title: A fast day
hookLine: Wednesday or Friday, a small fast
tomorrow: why does a table for two take more work than a table for one?

cards: Wednesday, mid-morning. Someone at the next desk passes on the pastry and drinks water instead. No speech about it, no sigh, no post.
If you didn't know, you'd never guess it was a fast day. So why skip lunch on purpose, and then hide it?
According to Jesus, the hiding is exactly the point, and it starts with a strange instruction about washing your face.

teach.b: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus talks about fasting the way you'd talk about something ordinary. He says “when ye fast,” not if. Then he gives one instruction: don't make a show of it.

teach.h: WASH THY FACE: KEEP IT SECRET.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: “But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret.”

The fast is real, but it's private, a conversation between a person and God, not a performance. Here's one to tell a friend: an old Christian teaching called the Didache already gives the habit a calendar.
It tells its readers to fast on Wednesday and Friday. That weekly rhythm still shows up today, in different shapes. Orthodox Christians keep Wednesdays and Fridays as fast days.
Catholics keep Friday as a day of penance, some by going without meat. Some Protestants choose a day of their own.

teach.h: SMALL, SAFE, AND TURNED TO GOD.
teach.b: A weekly fast can be small: one skipped meal, no meat, no sweets, no screens until evening. The going-without isn't the point by itself. The small hunger is a reminder, each time it shows up, to turn toward God.
And when going without food isn't safe, because of health, medicine, pregnancy, or a long shift in the heat, a fast can be from something else entirely. Quiet, small, and once a week.

how: Orthodox Christians keep Wednesdays and Fridays as fast days; Catholics keep Friday as a day of penance, some by going without meat; some Protestants keep a weekly fast day of their own choosing.

games.why: a fast can be from something else entirely when going without food isn't safe. the point is the turning toward God, kept quietly.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or reach for one nearby, and take one slow sip, tasting plain water the way someone might on a fast day. Then choose your day this week, and what you'll go without, something small and safe.
Let the next sip seal the choice, quietly, without telling anyone.

wordCard.voice: A fast day. One day a week of small going-without, kept quiet, with a hunger that points somewhere.
